127.t: Ragtime repertoire and Tiger Rag with Jack Carey
127.s: Rags played in those days (Maple Leaf, Panama, High Society) and Jack Carey's band being first to sing Tiger Rag.
127.q: Yeah, Maple Leaf was the famous, but I don't know, but Frog Legs. Climax. Climax. They played there. And this, what's that about the leaf you call it, Silver Leaf.

127.t: Tunes played by Jack Carey's band and 'number one'
127.s: Tiger Rag, That's a Plenty and others, and a piece Punch wrote that nobody plays.
127.ch: New Orleans halls and street bands
127.q: Well, Taggerad, That's A Plenty, Honeysuckle Road, Kranath Marbley, and what else? I was wondering if you were a kid, you know, a lot of head numbers that we know ourselves. Number one, called one.

127.t: The words sung to Tiger Rag again
127.s: Allen asks about the shouted words; Punch explains the 'hold that tiger' part.
127.ch: New Orleans halls and street bands
127.q: No, they just were regular singing all over the dance floor, you could just young hollering, Jack Carey, head of daughter, on the water, selling pork chops, two folk quarters, play Jack Carey, play Jack Carey, all that guys, you know.

127.t: Animal dance songs and singing Everybody's Doing It
127.s: Prompted about animal dances, Punch recalls older songs and sings Everybody's Doing It.
127.q: Um, everybody doing it? Doing it, doing it. Yeah, that's all mama. And, uh, they're coming to me now. Mama love Pa, Papa love Mama too. And, uh, beautiful dog. And, uh, oh, them the old ones.

619.t: Sadie, the Fosters and a run of tunes he played
619.s: A short exchange about the drummer married to Billy's sister, followed by Laurent reeling off waltzes and popular songs from his books.
619.ch: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
619.q: Chynee. Played with Celestan, yeah. Nancy, September in the Rain, Beautiful Dreamer. Remember of you, that's another one of mine.

619.t: More songs from the books, Copenhagen and Chinaman and Mabel
619.s: Laurent names more tunes, recites the words of Chinaman and Mabel, which he says he never copyrighted, and says he used to sing choruses.
619.ch: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
619.q: My old Kentucky home After the ball After the ball Was over After the ball Went down Oh man He used to play All of that stuff They'd pay you to play that Oh yeah They'd pay you to play that Till then Brown eyes Why you blue Body and soul Song of New Orleans Now they had Booth's New Orleans This is…

619.t: Waltzes and the Joplin rag book
619.s: Laurent and Russell look through his waltzes and a rag book that Charlie Love used to play, and Laurent says he played from memory.
619.q: I used to love that thing. Oh, I used to love that number. And you see, I used to commit all that to memory. I didn't want the music when I was playing out. I committed to memory.

8.t: Waltzes, polkas, quadrilles and street tunes of the early days
8.s: Dance repertoire of his youth, played mostly by ear; tunes such as Tiger Rag and a tango remembered by the interviewers.
8.q: Oh yeah, during that time we played waltzes, pox shots, we played shotties, and we played mazookas. Now when you played those- Then we used to play quadrilles, which people say Lancer, but written with quadrilles. You didn't call them figures set. They called figures no answers, you know. Lancer?…

8.t: Get Outta Here and Go On Home, and who first played Tiger Rag
8.s: The closing number of a dance, its link to Tiger Rag, and a discussion of who featured Tiger Rag first.
8.q: After the dance, we used to play a piece called Get Outta Here. Da-da-da. Da-da-da. Da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Get outta here. And gone home. See, the Lory went to work. What did he make out of that? What do you call it now? He does it.

8.t: Playing pop numbers at jazz dates
8.s: They always threw in a few pop numbers, such as Sister Kate.
8.ch: New Orleans style and bass playing
8.q: That's when I crips, we call crips, you know.

507.t: Learning of Treemonisha and Joplin's self-published opera
507.s: He recounts discovering the opera, wanting to stage it at New England Conservatory, and Joplin's struggle to publish it.
507.q: That amongst other things drew me to it. But the very fact – I knew about this opera when I was still very young. I just heard about it. Then I read Rudi Blesh’s book about ragtime. I learned a lot in that. I can’t remember when I read that. But then Martin Williams, who was really – he and Guy…

507.t: Red Back Book and forming the Ragtime Ensemble
507.s: He obtained a copy of the Red Back Book and formed the ensemble in 1972.
507.ch: Risë Stevens session and The Sting
507.q: this piece, because it is under copyright protection and it is not allowed to be performed in the one orchestration that has been done, by T. J. Anderson, a black composer who teaches here at Tufts University. There had been a performance of his arrangement of Tremonisha in Atlanta, and it was…

507.t: Rifkin's recording and Vera Lawrence's Joplin edition
507.s: He describes two events in the ragtime revival.
507.ch: Risë Stevens session and The Sting
507.q: rags. That was the first time anybody had recorded any ragtime. He did it, and he, in my opinion, although it’s very beautiful, he turned it too much into a really classical music. He did it all at very slow tempos, and he made it sound like Chopin or Liszt, and it certainly didn’t swing. His idea…

27.t: Show repertoire: Margie, Bugle Blues and marches on the bally
27.s: Tunes remembered from the shows, Lee's saxophone feature, and the marches played only outside on the bally, including Shouting Liza.
27.q: Yeah. "I kissed her or something on the back porch." [SINGS] That's the name of it, "Last Night On The Back Porch." The main one they used to play in them days was "Bugle Blues." That was the one that Lee used to feature

27.t: Tape change; the If You Don't Want Me blues
27.s: After a tape change, Phillips names one more blues they played before he joined.
27.q: "If you don't want me, why don't you tell me so?"

27.t: Repertoire of the Young shows in 1926
27.s: Phillips says everyone played the same tunes, such as I Love My Baby and Five Foot Two.
27.q: Yeah, the same... Everybody was doing the same thing. "I Love My Baby" and "Baby Won't You Please Come Home?" and "Five Foot Two and Eyes of Blue" and... "I Never Knew."

430.t: Scott Joplin rags played by the old bands
430.s: The old bands played Joplin rags straight; he played them by guessing before he read music.
430.q: But those bands, I mean Imperial and I just can't, I just can't recall these people, they're playing music, but these fellas, I mean, oh man, they played. You see the Scott Joplin books, all those rags, you don't hear none of that music. And them guys just took that music and played that music and…

430.s: The first tunes he heard were rags such as Maple Leaf Rag; he never saw one of them written.
430.q: No, I don't know. Mm-hmm. What's going to ask you about it? I wish I did because I never seen it. I never seen it written.

1.t: Reading bands versus ear players; the early repertoire
1.s: Only Piron, Robichaux, Desvignes and Celestin read music, and Barker lists tunes of the time and how vaudeville singers spread songs.
1.q: No. Nobody was reading, unless Piron and band, Robichaux, and they was playing, reading music. They put the music up there, because they could remember that limited repertoire they had. They put the music up there just to make sure. There was reading bands. Piron’s band, Sidney Desvignes’s band,…

1.t: Hippolyte Charles and the Maple Leaf band
1.s: He recalls Hippolyte Charles's band, which played Scott Joplin's music and took its name from Maple Leaf Rag.
1.ch: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
1.q: That's right. I have listened, but I can't call all the guys, man. I've been led by Hippolyte Charles, who was considered a great trumpet player one time, and the schools went into bad health, and some of these long, grandpa trouble, and they had to get up to home. One time he was highly recognized…

620.t: Other piano players and the popular repertoire
620.s: Thompson names George W. Thomas, Clarence Williams, Frank Crump and others; they played ragtime, blues and popular tunes, and he lists tunes he liked.
620.ch: First jobs and the piano scene
620.q: Played all the jazz. That's a shiny town. Down by the Old Mill Stream. Duh. Another song they used to play all the time. I used to like to play that. Span... In a little Spanish town.

620.t: Ham and Egg Blues and playing with Louis Keppard at a cabaret
620.s: He recalls Juby's Ham and Egg Blues, and a night with Louis Keppard at a cabaret near the French Market, playing Spanish Town repeatedly.
620.ch: First jobs and the piano scene
620.q: No, I... I never did take that. I had another... Another blues my brother used to play. I used to play all the time. They called the Ham and Egg Blues.

272.t: Repertoire of the Jazz Babies and his number 'Angry'
272.s: The band played popular tunes and its own numbers; Lizana recites the lyrics of 'Angry' as his number.
272.q: Pop or something. And then the stuff that we make up ourselves. The numbers that we make up. You may come in tonight. Let's see this. You know. And if you're going to play it good, we accept that.

272.t: The eight-piece jazz band drawn from the big band
272.s: The jazz band had eight pieces who could switch instruments and play anything, such as High Society and Livery Stable Blues.
272.ch: Baton Rouge big band and New York
272.q: Yeah, we could play anything. You see, I had enough readers and everything. That's a way you could switch around and play anything you wanted.

22.t: Black-composed numbers the ODJB featured and how the band sang them
22.s: La Rocca says he meant no harm to Black composers; the band featured Brown Skin, Mama's Baby Boy and Sister Kate, shouted them rather than sang, and played tunes by both Black and white writers.
22.ch: Piron, Clarence Williams and the ODJB repertoire
22.q: Well this will show that I did try to help the colored man out, and I had no malice or thought of doing anybody anything that was out of the way of being honest with anyone. We featured these numbers that rise to others. We featured Brown Skin, Who You Follow, which Will Rossiter published. That's…

22.t: Correcting the dates of the colored-melody numbers and novelty singing
22.s: The interviewer and La Rocca settle that the tunes were popular around 1918, played as novelties even in London, and La Rocca says he sang Margie before it was published.
22.ch: Piron, Clarence Williams and the ODJB repertoire
22.q: I got a role too. We played them all the way through London. They weren't in all.

276.s: Nash and an interviewer perform the old song; asked its date, Nash says it is much earlier than 1910.
276.q: Oh, no, that's way before that.

276.t: Junkman Rag, 'Shots and Shells' and a Civil War song
276.s: Allen asks about Junkman Rag, which Nash needs to practice; Nash sings part of 'Shots and Shells'/battlefield song, and does not know 'Just Before the Battle, Mother'.
276.q: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I want to get to build this bamboo Boys, our flag is done. Just bring the news to mother and tell her how did I love her And kiss how did sweet live for me For I'm not coming home Just saying that is no other Can take the place of mother And kiss how did sweet live for me For…

288.s: Charles says they played rhumbas and anything they could pick up.
288.q: You didn't play any rhombos? No. Well we played rhombos. You did? We just, you know, from the music. And then we put on whatever part we wanted in there, you see. But we played rhombos and music. In other words we played all kinds of music. Couldn't name a piece of music that we didn't play.

288.t: Playing rags (the Red Book) fast on trumpet and piano
288.s: Charles says his group could play Joplin rags from the Red Book at tempo, with Camilla Todd on piano.
288.ch: Society work, Camilla Todd and Storyville
288.q: Well, let me tell you one thing. We were the only one who could cut the Red Books. Mm-hmm. Cut Joplin music you're talking about. Yeah. What was that time? We were the only one.

138.t: Claiming the first ragtime band on the street; Perkins as reader
138.s: Laine says he had about the first ragtime band on the street; he recounts how his friend Perkins, a fine reader, came to play with him.
138.q: Was that before you were born, do you think? No, I was playing music then. I had a ragtime band. And I'm about the first one that ever had a ragtime band on the street.

138.t: Tunes at the parade, syncopated marches and Dave Perkins's sheet music
138.s: Laine can recall only a break and the march 'Underarm' that Perkins brought; they ragged straight marches like Stars and Stripes Forever.
138.q: Now, we used to play that underarm march. That was a wonderful march. Dave Perkins came down one night with a copy of that. And Dave Perkins was a first-class note reader. Really. That boy could take a sheet of music and go over it like nobody's business. Is that right? Well, he'd hum it. He'd hum…

385.t: Repertoire, the blues label, Joe Springer
385.s: He played every song but Dixieland, got labeled a blues player from Blue Harlem, and kept Joe Springer a long time.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: Yeah, a lot of blues. I got that's where my name got hung up as a blues player on account of Blue Harlem, 'cause that was the first record I made that did any selling, I mean it was among the first. And it sold very good, and like I said Fred Robins used it for his theme song, just that particular…

385.t: Atlantic and Gotham repertoire; Sidewalks of New York in chords
385.s: He confirms the repertoire and says Sidewalks of New York, in all chords, was an early experiment.
385.ch: On the road, Philadelphia and New York
385.q: - Drinkin' Beer? No. But as far as chord forming was concerned, that was is concerned, that was one of the first tunes I played, Sidewalks of New York, in all chords.

198.t: Using the A clarinet for older music and rags
198.s: Emile says the A clarinet was for music written in that key, including the old red-back rag books.
198.q: Yeah. They were in the key of A. All that stuff I used to know, but now I have to hear them to get to them again, see, but I've been with them. That's why I got my breaking in there. I ain't got no key to it. Played with the best and the worst. The best and the worst. Yeah.

621.t: Moving to New Orleans and the Kid Ory band repertoire
621.s: He joined Kid Ory's band, met jazz in New Orleans, and lists tunes such as Tiger Rag, St. Louis Blues and High Society.
621.q: when you got to New Orleans? Well, when I got to New Orleans, I joined the Kid Ora Band before we left Laplace, and then that's where we met jazz. We used to go to hill jazz in New Orleans, and we finally pick it up.

243.s: He explains the red books were school military march books, not ragtime books.
243.q: No, the military march books. Marches, I didn't know. Yeah, the school kids get them a lot of times. Now I mean I think you get hold of a red book when you get to about the second or third grade

248.t: Scott Joplin rags and the Red Back Book were hard to read
248.s: Dawson says playing Scott Joplin required real reading skill, and the two talk about Grace and Beauty, Maple Leaf and Allen's band.
248.q: Well, that, that, that was, uh, that was, um, Scott Joplin music was, you, you had to be well acquainted with music to play that kind. Because, you see, you're running up on, uh, you're running up on, uh, thirty-second and sixty-fourth, eight notes, tired notes, and, uh, thirty-second and…

622.t: How much the tunes themselves mattered
622.s: They discuss New Orleans versus Chicago-written tunes, built-in discipline of a standard repertoire, and martial brass-band tempo.
622.q: If you analyze the tunes that the Wolverines played, presumably unaffected, you'll find that when they play Royal Garden or Jasmine Blues, those are the weakest things they played. And they played them totally different from New Orleans. When they play a tune like Need Some Padding or Susie, which…

179.t: Favorite numbers and the first tunes learned
179.s: Sweet Georgia Brown, Lonesome Road, blues with Thomas; first number was Thomas's theme; Sensation Rag with Allen; waltzes, no quadrilles.
179.q: Oh well they used to play all numbers like uh, Sweet Georgia Brown and Look Down That Lonesome Road and all like that all that kind of numbers. Thomas used to play all blues and different stuff like that, different kind of blues.

172.t: Maple Leaf Rag and the Red Back Book
172.s: Ridgley says Tuxedo played little Maple Leaf Rag, which belonged to earlier players, and that Billy Marrero's Superior band used the Red Back Book. Newer bands change the tune.
172.q: We didn't have that. You know, Maple Leaf Rag, before my time, that was an old number. And they used to play it a whole lot before my time. But we didn't play too much of Maple Leaf Rag in our time, but they're playing it plenty since I quit. You see those fellas? And those fellas like rearranging…

182.t: Scott Joplin red books and Frog Legs
182.s: Tom bought four Scott Joplin red books, recalls Chris Kelly's cornet book, and says only Israel Garman could play Frog Legs; Ragtime Dance was the hardest music.
182.ch: Ragtime music and Scott Joplin books
182.q: Oh, these are them Scott Joplin books, them red books? Yeah. Well I bought four of them. Yeah? Chris Kelly got the cornet book and he died, and I never did got it the most. Yeah, did you? I wrote it to him, I never did got my cornet. I got the violin part down in the locker there somewhere. Yeah,…

252.t: Carrie Boote's minstrel show singing: Alexander, Dying Rag, Dollar Bill
252.s: Boote as a girl sang in minstrel shows; she recalls fragments of Alexander, Dying Rag and Dollar Bill.
252.q: That was a minstrel show we used to have. They called them minstrel shows then, you know. So I used to try to be an actress there. Mm-hmm.

255.t: Sheet music for every audience and his singing
255.s: His collection of popular and old songs lets him serve any crowd, with folk, foreign-language and Hank Williams numbers.
255.q: And this is from the show boats, some of them old numbers. I just get them and run over and I get the woods and so forth like that. Well, it's a lot of music. Get a lot of piano copies and different things like that. They got them all mixed in. Yeah. So you can look at any of them. Oh, yeah. Yeah.

623.s: Rarely rehearsed; tunes included Maple Leaf Rag, Tiger Rag, Memphis Blues, and Mack the Knife for a non-historical audience.
623.ch: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
623.q: I only tried rehearsing a couple of different times and I forget what the occasion was he just wanted to get a couple of tunes out I can remember rehearsing Memphis Blues with him I think probably the band was such a natural he could have just played it right off as a sort of a scholarly approach…

624.t: Fisher's repertoire: ragtime, Tiger Rag, Dixieland One Step
624.s: Allen asks what Fisher's band played: all ragtime, such as Tiger Rag, Tin Roof Blues and Dixieland One Step, for dances and all-day Sunday picnics.
624.ch: Fisher's band and Jack Laine's bands
624.q: And the tin roof blues. Bucket's got a hole in it. What was number? And, uh... Dixeland One Step? Huh? Dixeland One Step? Dixeland One Step. And, uh, old gray bonnet. Dixeland One Tip stuff like a little dance, a little party. And we used to go. And like me, I used to play out at different places…

625.s: The band played popular tunes, waltzes and rumbas; Celestin was featured on a few numbers and sang, with few original tunes.
625.q: That's all. He would be featured in this number, My Josephine. That was his number, you know. He would feature him in that number. Muscat rambled. Didn't he rambled? Numbers like that. They'd feature him in those numbers. Did he sing then? He sang. I just understand, sang a number. I've forgotten…

626.t: Ragtime and mixed repertoire of the Excelsior Band
626.s: The band mixed ragtime and all kinds of time, and its reputation reached across the South.
626.q: We used ragtime, all kind of time. We mixed it up all kind of way. That's what the people would like about it, you see? And all that foolishness is take with them, you know, and they'd follow their way. And when they mix up that stuff and they'd play it good and they'd sound good, you know. And it…

262.s: McNeil recalls waltzes and jump numbers such as Ain't She Sweet.
262.q: No, I can't think of any of the blues. I know some of the numbers, you know, I've forgotten them. They used to play a little bit, uh, uh, Ain't She Sweet, something like that, jazz number. Ain't She Sweet, see her walking down the street, you know, something like that. I can't recall that, you…

627.t: Early music boxes, records and 'Bill Bailey'
627.s: Cage had no music box growing up, only a cylinder-type one; they trade bits of 'Why Don't You Come Home, Bill Bailey' and 'Babe, Please Don't Let Me Fall'.
627.ch: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
627.q: Oh, I like that. I'm a whole piece. Did you listen to any... Please don't let me fall. What's that? Babe, please don't let me fall. Babe, please don't let me fall.

14.t: Favorite rags from the Red Book and what New Orleans bands played
14.s: Love names the Red Book rags he likes best and says New Orleans bands each played only a few of them.
14.q: Well I tell you I like them all. I played with one of them. But the best thing I liked, Frog Legs, Easy Winner, Chrysanthemum, Ophelia Ryan. They're real musical numbers.

38.t: Wickliffe's repertoire: Dixieland numbers, blues and rags
38.s: The band played Tiger Rag, Panama, blues in the trumpeter's key, popular tunes and rags with piano features.
38.q: Oh, well, we had Tiger Reg, and you know, with Fidgety Feet, and, well, four or five other numbers that were published for the first time. But, you know, the original Dixieland. Panama became a... Panama, oh yes, Panama. We played that, yeah, Panama.

126.t: Tunes played at the New York restaurant
126.s: They discuss the tunes the band played, including Oceana Roll, with Hardy unsure of titles the interviewer suggests.
126.q: Never, don't remember any of those. There's quite a number of other tunes that they were playing. Yeah, well, I think that they're the composition of some of those. Oceana Roll, was one of them. Oh, yeah.

181.t: Playing by head and ragtime tunes
181.s: Parker discusses bands playing by head, ragtime, made-up tunes like Funky Butt, and who made up tunes best.
181.q: All different tunes. Funky butt, take it away. Wonder why my baby gone tonight. All different tunes, you know? Made up, made up. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Who was the best...

274.s: Allen asks about music left from his father's time and favorite numbers; Labat names St. Louis Blues and High Society.
274.q: That's right. We'd be signing off. We'd play that, bye-bye Blackwood. We'd be playing because we started playing blackwood.

628.t: Low-down blues repertoire and the dirty dozens song
628.s: Williams lists the tunes bands played (Careless Love, Shake It and Break It, St. Louis Blues, Dinah) and describes a bawdy blues that got dancers shouting.
628.ch: Beginnings and early New Orleans scene
628.q: They played all these, uh, like, uh, the three sixes. See, because there's a copy from Chris Kelly, you see, all of them used to go from the blues, you see, and Careless Love, which was Chris Kelly, he was the man, he was the king of blues, because that was number D. He futures, you understand what…

23.t: What Armstrong played in the early saloons
23.s: Rose speculates about his repertoire: blues, popular pieces, Tiger Rag, Sister Kate, Bland songs.
23.q: And Louis always seemed to gravitate to the blues, anyway. Yeah. It was the kind of music that he really liked, and, and it, to a certain extent, put him out of step with the rest of the New Orleans musicians. Mm-hmm. Because they didn't play, uh, you know, blues as the main part of their action.…

629.t: How bands learned tunes and brass band tunes turned to jazz
629.s: Interviewer asks about learning new tunes and when brass band pieces such as Didn't He Ramble were jazzed.
629.q: The Butcher? The Butcher cut it down? Didn't he ramble? Didn't he ramble? Uh-huh. That's one of them. Didn't he ramble? Do you remember Muscat ramble? Oh, what's kept-

630.t: Charleston rhythm, added song parts and old repertoire
630.s: All bands played the same tunes; Chris Kelly added parts to songs, and he lists old titles like Basin Street Strut and his lost book.
630.q: You didn't have a special rhythm to them? No there wasn't nothing special because all of them could play the same tunes. They could all play that Charleston rhythm? All play that Charleston, all of them.

631.t: Playing without rehearsal, unnamed tunes and Ratification
631.s: Early groups played by ear with sharp ears; tunes had numbers not names and Ratification was the prestige number.
631.ch: Jack Laine and the New Orleans scene
631.q: Oh, well, Jack Lane was the cause of that. He called up all the kids and told them to meet at his house. We'd meet at his house and he had a pretty good-sized front room. So we'd play a couple of tunes and every man for himself. Mm-hmm. Of course, uh, you take in those days, the, the fellas that…

632.t: Bawdy tunes and Joe Watkins's dedication at Manny's
632.s: Repertoire of mildly suggestive songs at Manny's and Allen's memory of Watkins dedicating a blues.
632.ch: Parisian Room and Bourbon Street clubs
632.q: Uh huh. Uh huh. At Manny's they were playing largely for dancing. And people would make their requests and the band would try to, the band would try to play them. And I don't remember them doing any of their, uh mildly bawdy, uh tunes. Like down on the farm. Uh huh. And uh, oh there, there was a…

285.t: Tiger Rag and its earlier names
285.s: Lopez recalls Tiger Rag from about 1910 as Number Two or the CF and B-flat rag, and how it was played.
285.q: They called it Number 2. That was the one. Number 2 they called it. Number 2. And, uh, then the CF and B Rag. That was it. Tiger Rag. Oh, that...the Tiger Rag. Yeah. CF and B Flat. It started in the C, went to F, and then went to B Flat. Oh, Tiger Rag.

633.t: Playing a Bolden tune through the district and tune names
633.s: Passing through the district the country band played a Bolden piece to applause; he discusses unnamed band tunes and the Lizard on the Rail hit.
633.q: Through the district? Yeah. Now, we had done been made around all uptown, coming down, you know. And we had passed, we were coming through the district. That is, around Franklin Street and things. I mean, they had a place between Franklin and St. Louis. They'd run dead into the cemetery, like, you…

634.t: Old repertoire: blues, quadrilles, head numbers
634.s: Early bands made up their own tunes; the quadrille was going out when Happy started, and chardises were played by head.
634.ch: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
634.q: Well, blues, different songs, but most of those days, they made up their own songs, and they'd call it anything. And sometimes, about an hour afterwards, you'd go ask them to play that same piece that they did in a long ago, they couldn't be more played than a man or more.

571.t: Rose Leaf Rag and the Victory Walk brass band tune
571.s: They sort out the title Rose Leaf Rag and the brass band tune Victory Walk, which Lewis played with the Eureka and Eddie Jackson's Tuxedo band. Lewis does not know its origin.
571.q: Well, a lot of people, you see, we people out here, our pronunciation is funny. A lot of people think we say Victory Waltz, but it's Victory Walk.

635.t: 'Dixieland' versus jazz and ragtime; sharing sheet music
635.s: New Orleans bought music from St. Louis publishers, and downtown bands pooled money and exchanged books.
635.q: See? That's why I said they should have got the credit, but we beat them to the punch. Because we used to buy, because five, six guys in the band, seven guys in a string band was a big band. Everyone in that band would join that club for a dollar a month, didn't we? Right. Yeah. Like you get two of…

50.t: Ragtime, Melrose publishing and Al Rose
50.s: Ragtime was learned as jazz; Melrose published his pieces in 1925; a Rose took them to dinner.
50.q: Yes. And still has the music in the catalog. And not a, Mel, Mr. Mr. Melrose, there was somebody by the name of Rose, the man was named Rose himself, I think, that contacted us one day to take us out to dinner.

636.t: Repertoire shift to Bunk Johnson and George Lewis tunes
636.s: The Melbourne band's tunes came from Bunk Johnson and George Lewis records, replacing his earlier Oliver and Watters repertoire, played with a looser touch.
636.q: Oh yes, yes, yes. Most of the tunes were new to me actually. They were based on, mainly on the records, Bunk Johnson, George Lewis and those men made, whereas previously I'd been playing King Oliver, Lou Watter's sort of tunes.

292.t: Playing piano and the old songs she remembers
292.s: She names tunes she played and heard, such as Tiger Rag, Alexander's Ragtime Band and When the Saints, and Prohibition-era songs.
292.q: I used to play all these old time songs that I got here. I used to play all these old days. Margie, ain't we got fun? Bye-bye black boy. Waiting for the Robert E. Lee. Let a smile be your umbrella on a rainy day. Don't you hear that sometimes? Yeah, it's new. Sidewalks of New York. And take me back…

54.s: Bud sang Meet Me Tonight in Dreamland, Bill Bailey and Sometime You Caused Me to Wonder; McAllister promises to remember more.
54.ch: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
54.q: Well, we'll, we'll, we'll come back. I have a, there's another, uh, friend of mine here that, uh, that plays, uh, he's done retired now, too. He was with us, Louis Mazik. He says, I'll call him tomorrow. What is your... At least I go out to his home. He's the only one. What is your... That... Sax.…

195.t: Repertoire: Tiger Rag, Bugle Call Rag, blues and Hesitation Blues
195.s: Jazz standards and the blues were always in the repertoire, with songs like Gin Mill Blues and Little Rock Getaway. He recalls a hillbilly name for Hesitation Blues.
195.q: there i can't remember time when tiger rag and bugle call rag and we used to play clarinet marmalade and foot warmer we recorded foot warmer we and uh the louisiana is it five what is it paul yeah the only ones that ever make records of that as far as i know i may be mistaken here but it didn't…

637.t: Bolden's repertoire, range and open horn
637.s: The blues and other pieces Bolden played, including Tiger Rag, his high range, no mute, and no sheet music.
637.q: Yeah, yeah. He played all of them. I believe they say I could admit, but I believe he made that up. He played everything. Every piece was the side. Some of them was out there like you, but he played all that.

638.t: Father's tunes and old numbers played with Bunk Johnson
638.s: He recalls the tunes his father played, then old numbers and dances played with Bunk Johnson.
638.q: During that time, my father was playing. I didn't remember those numbers then because my father had been dead a long time. He died when I was ten years old. That'd make me remember none of the tunes. You wouldn't remember very much. No, but I know one tune he used to play all the time. I was small,…

476.t: Repertoire and banjo style in the early band
476.s: The band played Panama, Sister Kate and Shaking the Breaks in a mix of slow drags, foxtrots and waltzes; Harry played straight four chords with raps on solos.
476.ch: Early bands around Bay St. Louis
476.q: What? What, Dixieland? What the Dixieland style? What the time was? That was Panama. Panama. And Sister Kate. And, uh, I can't think of those pieces now. Sister Kate. Shaking the Breaks. Shaking the Breaks. That'd be one of y'all, man. Yeah. He was featured on them. Oh yeah.

25.t: Tempo, repertoire and Handy's Spanish beat
25.s: He describes the New Orleans bands' medium tempo and tunes, and speculates Handy got the Spanish beat in St. Louis Blues from Cuba.
25.ch: Chicago and the New Orleans bands
25.q: Well, uh, more, well they had, uh, their music was, uh, more on a medium beat. Most of their tunes were just, uh, what you might say, uh, medium two. It's their best tunes, such as the Weary Blues. And I don't know, Arty Matthews wrote Weary Blues, but, uh, they, uh, I don't know why they had it…

639.s: He likes both pop standards and old spirituals such as Closer Walk and Ole Miss, which Oliver played at Tulane Gym.
639.q: Oh, well, I think some numbers out of each category. Are good. Numbers, of course, like rumbas and things like that are kind of hard to do much with. But ordinarily, well, the pieces that have stuck, like My Blue Heaven and Out of the Popular Group, are always good. And Indiana, my home in Indiana,…

640.t: Singing with postwar British bands and early repertoire
640.s: Postwar revival bands gave her chances to sing; she lists tunes like Baby Doll and Young Woman Blues and making other songs fit Bessie's idiom.
640.ch: Singing in England and moving to North America
640.q: No because suddenly, don’t forget this was getting into the late 40s, and just after the war, and we were starting to have these bands sprouting up, all having listened to records and not always the best records because we had this rose thorn don’t forget that took a lot away from the fidelity, and…

347.t: Combo Ork book, repertoire of 5,500 songs and caring
347.s: He learned to read from the Combo Ork and Latin books, claims 5,500 songs including ethnic ones, and says one must learn to care.
347.ch: Charleston bands and learning to think
347.q: Yeah. And then I learned the Latin book too. I know that’s how I built my repertoire. You know, “Charmaine” “Maria Elena” — I know at least fifty-five hundred songs. Go as far back as you want. Ethnic songs too. Greek songs, Irish, Italian, Russian songs. I’m the only band that goes to Moscow that…

63.t: A repertoire of 150 arrangements and about 20 hits
63.s: He gets bored quickly, travelled with 150-175 pieces and 16-20 recognizable hits.
63.q: As many as we could do. I would get . . . My threshold for boredom is very high . . . very low, rather. I get bored very quickly. So we’d play a piece, and play it and play it, and I’d want to get a change. We ended up with a book of about—what we travelled with—a book of around 150, 175 pieces,…

367.t: Popular tunes played by the family band
367.s: Young recalls the family band played popular tunes such as St. Louis Blues, Stormy Weather and I'm Confessin'.
367.q: And it was a lot of popular, Confessin’…I’m Confessin’ [sings melody]. Confessing…I’m Confessin’. Well, a lot of things like that, we used to play them, my dad used to sing and play, he played good saxophone. And he was good…

113.t: Repertoire with Al Dennie and checking details of the early years
113.s: Asked what he played, he says stock arrangements and tunes like Honeysuckle Rose, playing chords by ear; the Dances check spellings and the length of his stays.
113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: Uh-huh, whatever, you know, 'Kansas City Kitty.' Let me see, what were some of these other tunes? Tunes like 'Judy,' you know --

65.s: With Agabama he was second voice and maraca player; they played guarachas, guajiras and son montuno in a more advanced style.
65.q: certain way, kind of halfbreed thing, more advanced that what Arsenio Rodriguez was playing and the other group was playing.

382.t: 'I'm Coming Virginia', an unusual song she still sings
382.s: She discusses the song's unusual 24-bar structure, its early recordings and keeping it in her repertoire forty years on.
382.ch: Early recordings and arrival in New York
382.q: Well "I'm Coming Virginia" was one of my own songs. That is, it's more of a thing that I had been doing, you know, previous to that.

641.t: Repertoire and time signatures of the early band
641.s: They played slow tunes and waltzes like Careless Love and Over the Waves, mostly in common time rather than marches.
641.ch: Instruments, first jobs and the regional scene
641.q: Well, we'd play slow tunes. Naturally, we all knew how to play slow tunes like "Careless Love" and "Over The Waves" was one of the tunes... "Over The Waves" sometimes we played in a waltz. I remember "When We Was Young," "At Three O'Clock In The Morning," "Let Me Call You Sweetheart," "Who's Sorry…

453.t: Armstrong's repertoire beyond the recorded pop tunes
453.s: Besides pop and show tunes, the band played older numbers like Shine and Black and Blue, which Armstrong had recorded before coming back to Chicago.
453.q: Yeah, we'd do -- he would do "Shine" and "Black and Blue" -- that's a tune -- that is a song that's really beautiful. Fats Waller 2

93.t: Slim and Shorty's routines and a Sweet Sue demonstration
93.s: Green recalls their numbers (Sweet Sue, Broadway Melody, Bugle Call Rag as the encore) and demonstrates Sweet Sue with humming and taps.
93.ch: Return to Atlanta and move north
93.q: So anyhow, we went out there, and Shorty and Slim, you know, and we did our "Sweet Sue" and the "Broadway Melody", and we really had to do an encore, which was the "Bugle Call Rag", you know. That's where we had a lot of pleasure.

566.t: Songs she sang with the Vendome band, including 'I'm In Love With You'
566.s: She sang 'If I Could Be With You', 'Trouble in Mind' and 'Blue Because Of You', and recites the lines of 'I'm In Love With You', which she never recorded. She liked the band improvising behind her.
566.q: Let's see, "Without your kind of blues, when there was someone else with you; I'm in love with you, that's why; every morning, noon and night, I'm in love with you, that's why". And I can't think of no more of it. And I used to love that song and everybody loved it. And I can't think of it.

72.t: Marching-band repertoire: Sousa, rags and overtures
72.s: The minstrel band played marches, swung rags like Rastus on the Trombone, overtures and Scott Joplin-style numbers.
72.q: Yeah, a number like that. And... Everything a march, you know. Well, I didn't know anything about... When they sang(?) to a march in (?), I didn't know anything about that. We didn't play that.

168.t: Repertoire and keys with the Marshall band
168.s: The group played blues and tunes like Shine and Chinatown, My Chinatown, mostly in C, B flat and F.
168.q: Oh, a lot of blues and -- and, of course, you know, like "Shine" maybe. I don't know -- a lot of tunes that I can't remember of that time. It's hard to remember right now. But I kept up with them, sure, whatever they did. "Chinatown, My Chinatown," "Charleston," and I can't remember some of those…

73.t: Gant's repertoire and accompanying Amanda Randolph
73.s: Gant played all the popular songs, accompanied Amanda Randolph, and could stride.
73.ch: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
73.q: Oh, yeah -- let me see, let me see -- Amanda Randolph was there, and he had to play for her. And, Amanda was -- let's see -- she sings pop -- some pop numbers medleys. So, you know --

81.t: Scott Joplin, Lottie Joplin's home and an early song that baffled him
81.s: Joplin is named as an early influence; songwriters later met in Lottie Joplin's home; Rasch asks about a song he first heard and did not understand.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: bunch of us songwriters had a meeting, in Scott Joplin's home in New York, and his wife was still living and a bunch of us songwriters met in her home, which I imagine we contributed to, Lottie Joplin, and well, so many of us -- honest to goodness, you wouldn't know what to do with the rest of us.

238.t: First songs and building a repertoire before recording
238.s: She describes the first songs she sang, such as Under a Blanket of Blue and The Object of My Affection, and the repertoire she had ready before recording.
238.q: Yeah, they had their own kitties, everybody had their own kitties. But that started, really started me to singing, you know. What I did, I used to get -- and then I started getting certain tunes, and what I would do, I'd get them and style them the way I'd want them, you know, I'd want to do it.…

13.s: Stocks and symphonic arrangements mixed with faked New Orleans tunes.
13.ch: Part Two: theaters and the Chicago scene
13.q: Oh, boy, that was a great band. We played a lot of stocks and big symphonic arrangements, they called them. Special arrangements. It was put out by the publishers. We called them symphonic arrangements. We had a lot of those, and small stocks.

112.s: He names a few songs played for dancing.
112.q: No, we played songs, we'd get songs together. There was a song called, "At That Million Dollar Ball", and I remember some old songs we played, "Fiddler, Fiddle on Your Violin", and we played these songs, and there's some more of them, "When the Midnight Choo-Choo Leaves for Alabam", like that kind…
